title: Count the Number of Computer Unlocking Permutations
statement:
A room holds `n = complexity.length` computers labelled `0` to `n - 1`, and the password of computer `i` has complexity `complexity[i]`. At the start only computer `0` is unlocked. Any other computer `i` can be unlocked only once some computer `j` with `j < i` and `complexity[j] < complexity[i]` is already unlocked.

An unlocking order is a permutation of `[0, 1, ..., n - 1]` that begins with computer `0`, where every later computer meets the rule above through a computer placed earlier in the order. Return how many unlocking orders exist, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Simulating every order works on tiny inputs, but there are up to (n − 1)! of them. The rule collapses to one comparison with computer `0`.

- If every other computer is strictly more complex than computer `0`, each one can be unlocked straight from computer `0` (its label `0` is below every other label). Computer `0` comes first and the other `n - 1` computers may follow in any order: (n − 1)! orders.
- If some computer `i >= 1` has `complexity[i] <= complexity[0]`, take the least complex computer among labels `1` to `n - 1`. Unlocking it needs a strictly smaller complexity, but computer `0` is not smaller and, by the choice of the minimum, no other computer is either. No order works, so the answer is `0`.

## Approach

1. Start with `ways = 1`.
2. For each `i` from 1 to `n - 1`: if `complexity[i] <= complexity[0]`, return `0`.
3. Otherwise multiply `ways` by `i` modulo `MOD`. After the loop `ways` is (n − 1)! modulo 10^9 + 7.
4. Return `ways`.

## Example 1, step by step

`complexity = [1, 2, 3]`. At `i = 1`, 2 > 1, so `ways = 1 · 1 = 1`. At `i = 2`, 3 > 1, so `ways = 1 · 2 = 2`. The answer is `2`: the orders `[0, 1, 2]` and `[0, 2, 1]`. In Example 2 the loop stops at `i = 1`, since 3 is not more than 3, and returns `0`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): one pass over the array.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- A tie does not unlock anything: the rule needs a strictly smaller complexity, so any value equal to `complexity[0]` makes the answer `0`.
- Count (n − 1)!, not n!: computer `0` is fixed at the front.
- Reduce modulo 10^9 + 7 after every multiplication. In JavaScript `ways * i` stays below 2^53 because `ways < 10^9 + 7` and `i < 10^5`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus 10^9 + 7 |
| `ways` | i! modulo `MOD` after computer `i` is checked |
| `i` | label of the computer being checked against computer `0` |

narration.3: ways will grow into (n - 1)!, one factor per computer after computer 0.
narration.4: Check every computer other than computer 0.
narration.5: Is this computer not strictly more complex than computer 0?
narration.6: Then the least complex such computer can never be unlocked, so no order exists.
narration.8: Computer i can be unlocked from computer 0 at any time, so multiply in the next factor of the factorial.
narration.10: Computer 0 leads and the rest may come in any order: (n - 1)! orders.
